stem.text: A function f has derivative \( f'(x) = 4x\left(x - 3\right) \) for all real x. On what open intervals is f increasing? Give a reason for the answer.

answer_key.label: f is increasing on the intervals \( (-\infty, 0) \) and \( (3, \infty) \), because \( f'(x) > 0 \) on each of those intervals.

worked_solution.text: The sign of f' can change only where \( f'(x) = 0 \) at \( x = 0 \) and \( x = 3 \).
worked_solution.rule_named: partition points of the sign chart

worked_solution.text: Testing one point in each piece gives \( f'(x) > 0 \) on the intervals \( (-\infty, 0) \) and \( (3, \infty) \) and \( f'(x) < 0 \) on the interval \( (0, 3) \).
So f is increasing on the intervals \( (-\infty, 0) \) and \( (3, \infty) \), because \( f'(x) > 0 \) on each of those intervals.
worked_solution.rule_named: sign of the derivative gives the direction of the function

options.label: f is increasing on the intervals \( (-\infty, 0) \) and \( (3, \infty) \), because it is positive there.
options.derivation: the right intervals, justified by a pronoun that never says which function is positive or negative

options.label: f is increasing on the interval \( (0, 3) \), because \( f'(x) > 0 \) on that interval.
options.derivation: the sign of f' read backwards, so the pieces where f' has the opposite sign are reported

options.label: f is increasing on the interval \( (\frac{3}{2}, \infty) \), because f' is increasing there.
